name: Infective Endocarditis

veryLikely: Viridans group streptococci (native valve, subacute presentation)
Staphylococcus aureus (acute presentation, IV drug use)
likely: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (prosthetic valve, particularly early post-operative)
possible: HACEK organisms and other fastidious organisms (culture-negative endocarditis)
pathogens.why: Pathogen likelihood depends heavily on the clinical context: native valve subacute disease points toward viridans streptococci, acute presentations and IV drug use point toward S. aureus, and prosthetic valve infection (especially early) points toward coagulase-negative staphylococci — empiric choice should be tailored to this context pending blood culture results.

investigations.test: Blood cultures (≥3 sets from separate sites, before antibiotics)
investigations.why: The single most important diagnostic step — identifies the organism and is a major Duke criterion; false-negative cultures from premature antibiotics significantly complicate diagnosis and management.

investigations.test: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), followed by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) if TTE inconclusive or high suspicion persists
investigations.why: Identifies vegetations, abscess, or valve destruction — a major Duke criterion and essential for surgical planning.
Screens for new conduction abnormalities (e.g., new heart block), which can indicate perivalvular abscess extension.
Supports overall assessment of inflammatory burden and any renal involvement (e.g., immune complex glomerulonephritis).

reason: a history of injection drug use

raises strong suspicion for infective endocarditis. Multiple blood cultures must be drawn before starting empiric antibiotics, since cultures drawn after antibiotic initiation may become falsely negative and complicate both diagnosis (Duke criteria) and subsequent targeted therapy.
